title: Main Idea and Details
bigQuestion: How do you find the one thing an article most wants you to know?

story.title: The Sentence That Holds the Hive Together
story.kicker: A class reads an article about honeybees, and one student finds the sentence that every other sentence leans on.
paragraphs: Mr. Bell hands out an article called "A City in a Box." It is about honeybees. Devon groans. It is two whole pages. There are words like colony and nectar. "Read the first paragraph," Mr. Bell says. "Then stop. Find the sentence that the other sentences hold up."

Devon reads. One sentence says a hive can hold many thousands of bees. Another says every bee has a job. Another says worker bees fly out to flowers and bring back nectar. Another says guard bees stand at the door. Devon frowns. Which one is the big one?

Then he sees it. The second sentence says, "A honeybee hive works like a busy city, and every bee has a job." The nectar sentence is a job. The guard sentence is a job. The thousands of bees are the people of the city. Every other sentence is an example of that one.

"That's the main idea," Devon says out loud. Mr. Bell nods. "The rest are details. They hold it up like legs hold up a table." Devon reads the second page. It has a heading, a picture of a waggle dance, and a caption. Now the two pages do not feel so long.

Before the bell, Mr. Bell asks the class to say the whole article in two sentences. Devon writes: "A hive is like a city where each bee has a job. Workers gather nectar, guards protect the door, and the queen lays the eggs." He did not copy one line. He got it.
story.think: Devon found the main idea by asking which sentence the others held up. Where else could you use that question?

lessons.title: The Topic Is Not the Point
lessons.mainIdea: The topic is what a text is about in a word or two; the main idea is what the text says about that topic.
reading: Read this short paragraph. "Dogs need a walk every day. A walk keeps a dog's legs strong. It lets the dog sniff and see new things. A dog that walks is calmer at home." What is it about? Dogs. That is the *topic*. The topic is just the subject, one or two words.

Now ask a harder question. What does the paragraph say about dogs? It says dogs need a walk every day. That is the *main idea*. The main idea is a whole sentence. It is the point the writer wants you to walk away with.

Here is a quick test. If your answer is one word, you found the topic. If your answer is a sentence with a verb, you found the main idea. "Honeybees" is a topic. "A honeybee hive works like a busy city" is a main idea.

words.d: the subject of a text, said in one or two words
the most important point a text makes about its topic, said in a sentence

look.title: Two Answers for One Paragraph
look.text: Picture a paragraph about the school lunchroom. It says the lunchroom is loud. It says four hundred kids eat there at once. It says the tables are close together. It says the tile floor bounces every sound. A student says the topic is "the lunchroom." Another says the main idea is "The lunchroom is loud because so many kids eat in a hard, crowded room."
look.prompt: Why is the second answer a main idea and the first answer only a topic?

check.q: What is a topic?
choices: The last sentence of a text
The subject of a text in a word or two
A fact that proves the point
check.why: The topic is just the subject, like dogs or honeybees. It is not a whole point.

check.q: Which one is a main idea, not a topic?
choices: Dogs need a walk every day
check.why: A main idea is a whole sentence that makes a point. The other three are one- or two-word topics.

check.q: You answer with a single word. What did you most likely find?
check.why: One word is a topic. A main idea needs a sentence with a verb.

lessons.title: Details Hold Up the Idea
lessons.mainIdea: Supporting details are the facts, examples and reasons that prove or explain the main idea.
reading: Think of a table. The top is the main idea. The legs are the *details*. "A honeybee hive works like a busy city." That is the top. "Workers gather nectar. Guards stand at the door. The queen lays eggs." Those are the legs. Take the legs away and the top falls.

A detail can be a fact, an example, a number or a reason. In the dog paragraph, "a walk keeps a dog's legs strong" is a reason. "It lets the dog sniff new things" is an example. Each one answers the question, "How do you know?"

Not every sentence is a detail. Some sentences are just extra. If a paragraph about bee jobs says, "Bees are yellow and black," that sentence does not hold up the idea. Good readers sort the legs from the extra.

words.d: a fact, example or reason that supports the main idea
to hold up or prove; details support the main idea

look.title: One Idea, Three Legs
look.text: Chicago winters are hard on sidewalks. Water gets into tiny cracks and freezes. Ice takes up more room than water, so the cracks get wider. Salt trucks help drivers, but salt eats into the concrete too. By spring, many blocks have new holes.
look.prompt: Which sentence is the main idea? Name two details that hold it up.

check.q: What do supporting details do?
choices: They prove or explain the main idea
check.why: Details are the legs that hold up the main idea. They answer, "How do you know?"

check.q: In the sidewalk paragraph, which sentence is a detail?
choices: Chicago winters are hard on sidewalks
Water gets into tiny cracks and freezes
check.why: The freezing water is a fact that shows how winter hurts sidewalks. The first choice is the main idea itself.

check.q: A paragraph is about bee jobs. Which sentence is extra, not a detail?
choices: Guard bees stand at the door
check.why: Color does not explain a bee's job. The other three sentences all hold up the idea about jobs.

lessons.title: The Main Idea of a Whole Article
lessons.mainIdea: A whole article has one main idea, and each paragraph's main idea is a detail that supports it.
reading: One paragraph has a main idea. A whole article has one too. Think of a bigger table. The article's main idea is the top. Each paragraph's main idea is a leg. The details in each paragraph are the small screws that hold each leg on.

Take the bee article. Paragraph one says every bee has a job. Paragraph two says the hive stays warm because bees shiver together. Paragraph three says bees dance to share where flowers are. Put them together: "Honeybees survive because they work as a team." That is the article's main idea.

To find it, read the title. Read the first and last paragraphs closely. Then ask what all the paragraph ideas have in common. The answer is often stated near the start or the end. Sometimes it is not stated at all, and you must build it yourself.

words.d: a short piece of nonfiction writing about one subject
shared by all; what several ideas have that is the same

look.title: Where Writers Put the Main Idea
look.cite: counted for this lesson, in ten short model articles written for this course
look.prompt: Based on these counts, where should you look first for an article's main idea?

check.q: How does a paragraph's main idea relate to the whole article?
choices: It is a detail that supports the article's main idea
It is always the same as the article's main idea
It has nothing to do with the article
check.why: Each paragraph's idea is a leg under the article's big idea.

check.q: Three paragraphs say bees have jobs, keep warm together, and dance to share news. What do they have in common?
check.why: Jobs, shivering together and dancing to share are all teamwork. That shared idea is the article's main idea.

check.q: Where is an article's main idea most often stated?
choices: Near the start or the end
check.why: Writers usually state the main idea early or in the closing. The middle mostly holds details.

lessons.title: A Summary in Your Own Words
lessons.mainIdea: A summary tells the main idea and the biggest details in a few sentences, in your words, not the author's.
reading: Devon said a two-page article in two sentences. That is a *summary*. A summary is short. It gives the main idea and the most important details. It leaves out the small stuff, the jokes and the repeats.

Here is the trap. Copying a sentence is not a summary. If you write the author's words, you did not show that you understood them. Close the book. Say the idea out loud to a friend. Then write what you said. Those are your own words.

Try it with this: "Sea otters float on their backs. They hold hands while they sleep so they do not drift apart. They also wrap themselves in kelp, a kind of seaweed." A summary: "Sea otters use holding hands and kelp to stay in place while they sleep." Short, true, and in your words.

words.d: a short retelling of the main idea and biggest details in your own words
a large brown seaweed that grows in the ocean

look.title: Copy or Summary?
look.text: Two students summarize the same paragraph about the moon. Ana writes: "The moon has no air, so there is no wind. The moon has no air, so footprints stay for a very long time." Luis writes: "Because the moon has no air or wind, marks on it last a very long time." The original paragraph had the exact sentence, "The moon has no air, so there is no wind."
look.prompt: Which student wrote a real summary? What did the other student do instead?

check.q: What belongs in a summary?
choices: The main idea and the biggest details
check.why: A summary is short and keeps only what matters most.

check.q: Why is copying a sentence not summarizing?
choices: The author's sentences are always wrong
It does not show you understood the idea
check.why: Putting the idea in your own words proves you understood it. Copying skips that step.

check.q: Which is the best trick for using your own words?
choices: Say the idea out loud with the book closed
Change one word in each sentence
check.why: When you say it aloud without looking, the words that come out are yours.

lessons.title: What It Says and What It Hints
lessons.mainIdea: A text says some things explicitly, right on the page, and implies other things that you must figure out from clues.
reading: Read this. "Maya grabbed her umbrella and her boots before she left for school." Does the sentence say it is raining? No. It says umbrella and boots. But you know. The text *implies* rain. To imply is to hint without saying.

Now read this. "It was raining hard, so Maya grabbed her umbrella." This time the text says it. It is *explicit*, right there in plain words. Good readers know the difference. When a teacher asks, "What does the text say?" she wants the explicit part. When she asks, "What can you tell?" she wants what it implies.

Check your hints against the words. If a text says a bee "shivers to make heat," you may infer bees can be cold. You cannot infer bees have fur. Nothing on the page points to that. A good inference always has a clue you can point to.

words.d: said plainly, right on the page
to hint at something without saying it directly
to figure out something the text does not say, using clues

look.title: Find the Hint
look.text: The bus was late again. Jamal checked his watch three times. He shifted his backpack from one shoulder to the other. When the bus finally came, he ran the last few steps and dropped into a seat with a long breath.
look.prompt: What does the text say explicitly about the bus? What does it imply about how Jamal feels?

check.q: A text says, "Maya grabbed her umbrella and boots." What is implied?
check.why: Umbrella plus boots are clues for rain. The text hints it without saying it.

check.q: What does explicit mean?
check.why: Explicit information is right there in the words, like "It was raining hard."

check.q: A text says bees shiver to make heat. Which inference is fair?
check.why: Shivering for heat points to cold. Nothing on the page points to fur, fear or snow.

sections.title: Reading the Parts of a Page

lessons.title: Headings and Bold Words
lessons.mainIdea: Headings tell you what a section is about, and bold words point to terms the author wants you to learn.
reading: Open a science book. The page is not one gray block. There is a big title. Under it are smaller titles, like "How Bees Find Flowers" or "Inside the Hive." Those are *headings*. A heading is a label for a chunk of text. It tells you the topic of that chunk before you read it.

Some words on the page are darker and thicker than the rest. They are in *bold*. Writers put a word in bold when it is a key term. Often the meaning is right there in the same sentence. "Bees carry *pollen*, a yellow dust from flowers, on their legs." The bold word plus the words after it give you a free definition.

Use these parts before you read. Run your eyes down the headings. Now you know the map of the article. Then read the bold words. Now you know the vocabulary. You have not read a full paragraph yet, and you already know a lot.

words.d: a short title above a section that tells what the section is about
dark, thick letters that make a key word stand out
a fine yellow dust that flowers make; bees carry it from flower to flower

look.title: A Map Made of Headings
look.text: An article about the Chicago River has these headings: "A River That Ran Backward," "Why the City Changed It," "The River Today." A student has not read one paragraph. But she says, "I bet this is about how people changed the river's direction, and what it is like now."
look.prompt: How could she guess the article's shape before reading it? Which heading would you read first if you wanted to know why the change happened?

check.q: What does a heading do?
choices: It tells the topic of the section under it
check.why: A heading is a label for the chunk of text below it.

check.q: Why do writers put a word in bold?
choices: Because it is a key term to learn
Because it is the longest word
check.why: Bold marks a key term, and its meaning is often given in the same sentence.

check.q: You read the headings and the bold words before reading the article. What do you gain?
choices: Nothing; you must read every word first
A map of the topics and the key vocabulary
check.why: Headings give the map; bold words give the vocabulary. Then the article is easier.

lessons.title: Captions, Diagrams, Maps and Sidebars
lessons.mainIdea: Pictures, diagrams, maps and sidebars carry facts that the paragraphs may not say, so read them as part of the text.
reading: Under the picture of the waggle dance is one line of small print: "A worker bee dances in a figure eight to show where flowers are." That is a *caption*. Many readers skip captions. That is a mistake. The caption often has a fact that is nowhere else on the page.

A *diagram* is a drawing with labels. A diagram of a bee might label the wings, the stinger and the pollen baskets on its legs. A map shows where. A map of Illinois might mark the towns with the most beekeepers. Read a map the way you read a sentence: look at the title, the labels and the key.

A *sidebar* is a box of text set off from the rest, often with its own color. It tells a small side story, like "How Honey Is Made." Sidebars are extra, but they are often the most interesting part. Read the picture, the caption, the diagram and the box. All of it is the text.

words.d: the words under or beside a picture that explain it
a drawing with labels that shows the parts of something
a box of extra text set off from the main article

look.title: Where the Facts Hide
look.cite: counted for this lesson, in a two-page model article on honeybees written for this course
look.prompt: How many facts would a reader miss by reading only the paragraphs? Is that a lot?

check.q: What is a caption?
choices: The words that explain a picture
check.why: A caption sits under or beside a picture and tells what it shows.

check.q: In the fact count, how many facts sit outside the paragraphs?
check.why: Captions (4) plus diagram labels (6) plus the sidebar (3) make 13 facts outside the paragraphs.

check.q: A student skips every diagram and caption. What happens?
choices: He reads faster and misses nothing
He misses facts that are only in those parts
He finds the main idea faster
check.why: Captions and diagrams often carry facts the paragraphs never state.

lessons.title: Skim First, Scan for Answers
lessons.mainIdea: Skimming means reading fast to get the general idea; scanning means moving your eyes to find one specific thing.
reading: You have two minutes and a four-page article. Do not start at word one. *Skim* it. Read the title, the headings, the first sentence of each paragraph, and the last paragraph. Your eyes move fast. You are looking for the big shape, not the small facts. In two minutes you know what the article is about.

Now the teacher asks, "How many eggs can a queen bee lay in a day?" You do not skim for that. You *scan*. Scanning is hunting for one thing. Your eyes jump down the page looking for a number, or the word "eggs," or the word "queen." You ignore everything else until you land on it.

Skim to learn the shape. Scan to find a fact. Read closely to understand. Good readers use all three, and they choose on purpose. If someone says, "Just find the date," scan. If someone says, "Tell me what this is about," skim, then read.

words.d: to read quickly to get the general idea
to move your eyes over a page looking for one specific word or fact

look.title: Two Jobs, Two Ways to Read
look.text: Rosa has a sheet with two jobs. Job one: "In one sentence, what is this article about?" Job two: "On what date did the beekeeper first open the hive?" For the first job she reads the title, the headings and the first sentence of each paragraph. For the second she runs her finger down the page looking for a month name.
look.prompt: Which job did Rosa skim for, and which did she scan for? How can you tell?

check.q: When you skim, what are you looking for?
choices: The general idea of the text
check.why: Skimming is fast reading for the big shape, not for one small fact.

check.q: The teacher asks how many eggs a queen lays in a day. What should you do?
choices: Scan for a number or the word eggs
check.why: Scanning hunts for one specific fact. You jump to the number or key word.

check.q: Which parts do you read when you skim?
choices: Title, headings, first sentences, last paragraph
check.why: Those parts give the shape of the text without reading it all.

lessons.title: Ask Before, During and After
lessons.mainIdea: Good readers ask questions before they read, while they read and after they finish, and then check whether the text answered them.
reading: Before Devon read the bee article, he looked at the title and asked, "Why is a hive like a city?" That question gave him a reason to read. It is a *before* question. Look at the title and the pictures. Ask what you already know. Ask what you want to find out.

While reading, keep asking. "Wait, what does colony mean?" "Why do the bees shiver?" "Does this fit with what the first paragraph said?" These *during* questions catch you when you drift. If you cannot answer a during question, stop and reread. That is not slow reading. That is smart reading.

After the last line, ask again. "Did I find out why a hive is like a city?" "What was the main idea?" "What surprised me?" If your before question never got answered, that is worth knowing too. It might be your next research question.

words.d: a large group of the same kind of animal living together, like all the bees in one hive
to read something again, often to fix a part that did not make sense

look.title: One Reader's Questions
look.text: Before: Why do bees dance? During: Is the figure eight the same as the waggle? Why does the sun matter to the dance? After: So the dance points toward the flowers, and the sun is the compass. I still do not know how far the flowers are. What tells them that?
look.cite: a reader's notes, written for this lesson
look.prompt: Which of the reader's questions got answered? Which one could become a research question?

check.q: What is a good before question?
choices: What do I want to find out from this title?
check.why: Before questions come from the title and pictures and give you a reason to read.

check.q: You cannot answer a during question. What should you do?
choices: Ask a friend for the answer
check.why: Rereading fixes the part that did not make sense. That is what strong readers do.

check.q: The reader's before question never got answered. What does that tell her?
choices: It could be her next research question
check.why: An unanswered question is a place to keep looking, not a failure.

review.q: What is the difference between a topic and a main idea?
choices: A topic is a sentence; a main idea is a word
A topic is the subject; a main idea is the point made about it
A topic is always at the end
review.why: Topic: honeybees. Main idea: a hive works like a busy city.

review.q: In the class story, why was "every bee has a job" the main idea?
choices: Every other sentence was an example of it
review.why: The nectar, guard and queen sentences all held it up like table legs.

review.q: Which is a supporting detail for "A hive works like a city"?
choices: Guard bees stand at the door
review.why: Guards at the door is a job, which shows how the hive is like a city.

review.q: What is wrong with copying a sentence as your summary?
choices: Nothing; it is the best way
It does not show that you understood
review.why: A summary must be in your own words to prove you got the idea.

review.q: "Jamal checked his watch three times." What does this imply?
review.why: Checking a watch again and again is a clue that he is worried about being late.

review.q: Which part of a page gives you the meaning of a key term in the same sentence?
review.why: Writers bold a key term and often define it right there.

review.q: You need to find one date in a long article. Which is fastest?
review.why: Scanning hunts for one specific thing, like a number or a date.

review.q: Why ask a question before you read?
choices: It gives you a reason to read and something to look for
review.why: A before question turns reading into a search, which keeps you focused.
